inputs.original_text: This account treats security as Israel’s freedom to keep using force and asks the US to hold firm, while casting Iran’s demands as coercion. That framing leaves out the central question: whether a ceasefire can protect civilians and reduce the risk of further violence, rather than preserve one side’s military options. The Strait of Hormuz matters, but invoking its security should not become a blanket excuse to reject negotiation or impose terms through US pressure. A durable settlement needs to address the power imbalance and protect people on all sides—not just reassure governments that they can keep escalating.
inputs.modified_text: The real test of any ceasefire is whether it protects civilians and prevents more violence—not whether Israel retains room to use force. The US should not use its influence to entrench a power imbalance or turn security concerns around the Strait of Hormuz into an excuse to shut down negotiations. A lasting settlement must prioritize people on all sides, not simply preserve governments’ ability to escalate.
